segments.speaker: A
segments.text: Welcome back to our study of Machine Learning Systems. Last time we ran training backwards — the iron law says time is work over rate, and every trick in that chapter moved the rate side. Faster silicon, better kernels, higher efficiency. The work term itself, the six-P-D operation count, looked untouchable.

visual.title: The selection inequality as two bars
visual.alt: Top bar: full-data training time. Bottom bar: the selection pipeline's bill -- scorer pass plus training on the subset. Selection is a win only while the bottom bar stays shorter at matched quality; the margin between them is the saving, and scorer cost is what eats it.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: And this chapter touches it. Data selection is the only lever in the book so far that shrinks the numerator. Every token costs the same forward pass, backward pass, and optimizer update — whether it teaches anything or is a duplicate of a duplicate. So if the marginal tokens carry almost no signal, deleting them is the cheapest FLOP in the whole system.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: Which sounds like an obvious win. But the chapter opens with a wall, not a win. Walk me through the data wall.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: GPT-2's corpus, WebText, is about forty gigabytes of text — roughly ten billion unique tokens. The Chinchilla-fitted balance wants about twenty unique tokens per parameter. For a one-and-a-half-billion-parameter model that's thirty billion unique tokens needed, against ten billion supplied. The corpus is a third of the fit.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: So the run covered the gap by repetition — it re-read the same corpus roughly seventeen times. One hundred sixty-seven billion tokens processed, of which about a hundred fifty-seven billion were tokens the model already owned. And GPT-3 sat even deeper, at about one-point-seven tokens per parameter.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: Right. And here's the subtlety — repeating isn't free filler. Every repeat still costs a full training step. It buys less each pass, because the marginal learning signal decays. The chapter models information content as growing only logarithmically with data — so the marginal information-compute ratio falls as one over the dataset size. Each doubling of the corpus halves what the next FLOP learns.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: ICR — that's the unit price the chapter puts on data. Learning gained per FLOP spent. And they actually measured it: a half-size ImageNet coreset gained four-point-five points against full data's five, in one epoch. Slightly worse score, half the compute — which is one-point-eight times the ICR.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: That example is doing real work. It shows the trade isn't "prune and lose nothing" — it's "accept a small quality delta for a large compute delta, and check whether the exchange rate is good." Which brings us to the law of the chapter.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: The selection inequality. Selection time plus training time on the subset must be less than training time on the full set — at matched quality and coverage. It's a break-even, not a bonus.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: And the worked case shows how easily it clears: a hundred twenty-eight thousand image coreset — ten percent of ImageNet — where the scoring pass costs at most a third of an epoch, and subset training makes every one of a hundred epochs ten times cheaper. The scorer could cost almost the whole run and it would still win on time.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: But the inequality has a second clause people forget — matched quality AND coverage. That ten-percent subset can hit top-one accuracy while quietly deleting a rare class. Which is why the chapter adds coverage floors: minimum representation per class or slice, applied before the score ranking gets to spend the budget.

visual.title: Coverage floors constrain the score ranking
visual.alt: A score-ranked pool (left) under a three-slot budget and a one-per-slice floor: the rare class keeps its floor slot even with the lowest score, displacing the third-ranked common example. Floors spend opportunity cost on representativeness; a budget smaller than the summed floors is infeasible.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: Floors are a constraint layer, not a quality tweak. If the summed floors exceed the budget, the plan is infeasible — no ranking can fix it. And there's an honest cost: every forced low-score keep displaces a high-score one.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: Let's hit the actual toolbox. Static pruning first — the unambiguous win is deduplication. On the GPT-2 corpus, dedup reads forty gigabytes once — six seconds at seven gigabytes per second on NVMe — and keeps a hundred twenty-eight hash MinHash signature per document, about four gigabytes of RAM. The return is three to fourteen hours of the four-day run and tens of kilowatt-hours, at essentially zero accuracy cost, because the deleted tokens were literally copies.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: Everything after dedup trades signal for cost — quality pruning, coresets. Then the dynamic levers: curriculum learning, which reorders samples by difficulty because a hard case is noise to an unstabilized model. And active learning, which is the same inequality paid in dollars — score the unlabeled pool, send the top-k to an oracle, retrain, repeat. The worked ROI: a million unlabeled scans at five dollars a label, and the active strategy reaches the target with fifty thousand labels — two hundred fifty thousand dollars, against five million naive.

visual.title: The active-learning loop and who pays each stage
visual.alt: Score the unlabeled pool, query the top-k for the oracle, add the new labels, retrain, repeat. The label bill sits at the oracle; the compute bill sits at scoring and retraining -- both enter the inequality against a budget-matched random baseline.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: But the scorer bill is per-round, and rescore-the-whole-pool each round reintroduces the cost the loop was avoiding. The inequality survives only if per-round scoring stays sublinear in pool size.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: Then the unlabeled-data levers. Semi-supervised and self-supervised trade extra compute for fewer labels. And the foundation-model version: pay ten thousand GPU-hours of pretraining once, then fifty per fine-tune, versus a thousand per task from scratch. The break-even is ten-point-five — so at least eleven downstream tasks before prepaid wins.

visual.title: Foundation amortization: prepaid versus scratch
visual.alt: From-scratch training costs 1,000 GPU-hours per task; the pretrained path pays 10,000 once and 50 per fine-tune. The lines cross at N = 11 downstream tasks -- below it, self-supervision is the more expensive option; above it, the per-task marginal cost is ~20x lower.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: Now the part I liked best — the engineering tax. Selection removes accelerator work but adds host work, and the worst of it is the random-access penalty. A retained subset scattered across shards turns sequential reads into thousands of little random reads. Realized bandwidth on four-kilobyte reads: three hundred seventy-five times worse on spinning disk, fourteen times on SATA SSD, under two on NVMe.

visual.title: The random-access penalty by storage tier
visual.alt: A retained subset scattered across shards turns sequential reads into small random reads. Realized-bandwidth loss for 4 KB reads: ~375x on HDD, ~14x on SATA SSD, under 2x on NVMe. Stream-and-discard keeps sequential speed but still reads every corpus byte; materialized subset shards are what make the saving physical.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: Which produces the practical rule: a ten-percent subset only saves reads when it's materialized into its own shards. Stream-and-discard filtering keeps sequential speed but reads a hundred percent of the bytes to deliver ten percent of the samples.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: And data echoing sits on the other side — when the host is the slow stage, re-using a prepared batch twice from cache fills the accelerator's idle slots. For the input-bound ResNet-fifty the GPU sat half idle; echo factor two closes the gap. But — and this is the fallacy — echo recovers stranded cycles. If the host already outruns the GPU, echoing recovers nothing.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: Finally the economics. Total data cost includes licensing, annotation, storage — routinely dwarfing compute. And amortization decides whether a fixed curation cost is a loss or a multiplication: the book's dedup pipeline is negative eighty-two percent ROI on its first run and positive eight hundred nine percent by the fiftieth. Same pipeline, same per-run saving — only the divisor changes.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: So the chapter's discipline, end to end: data selection is the only lever that shrinks O. But it only counts when score-plus-subset beats full at matched quality and coverage, the data path is engineered so the fix doesn't move the bottleneck, and fixed costs amortize across the runs that share them.

visual.title: The selection inequality as two bars
visual.alt: Top bar: full-data training time. Bottom bar: the selection pipeline's bill -- scorer pass plus training on the subset. Selection is a win only while the bottom bar stays shorter at matched quality; the margin between them is the saving, and scorer cost is what eats it.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: Same discipline as training, one layer upstream — measure value against cost, prove the overhead fits the budget, attack the limiting term. Next time: data engineering — the pipeline that feeds all of this.
